subject: English Language

questions.prompt: Add a tag to “Samson married Rukia last year.”
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
The statement is positive past simple; use negative did and pronoun he.

questions.prompt: A Mathematics test will occur every Friday from today. What activity is this?
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
Every Friday specifies repetition, even though the routine begins in the future.

questions.prompt: “By this time tomorrow I will have finished my homework” means what?
questions.answer: B — By that time I will finish the homework, is the closest option: it will already be completed by the stated time.
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
Future perfect will have finished expresses completion no later than the reference time, rather than starting or still working.

questions.prompt: “The guests are staying with us for two months” expresses what?
questions.answer: D — Their stay will last temporarily, is the best answer for the limited duration. A also correctly recognises a current stay.
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
For two months limits the stay, so B, permanent, is false and C, already completed, is false. Present continuous can describe the current temporary situation.

questions.prompt: How should you politely oppose a claim that girls’ education is unimportant?
questions.answer: B — I can see your point. But …
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
This acknowledges the speaker before presenting disagreement; the alternatives insult the speaker or agree with the claim.

questions.prompt: Which opening fits a formal telephone conversation?
questions.answer: A — Hello, am I speaking to Jimmy?
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
It greets politely and checks the recipient’s identity; the others are abrupt or assume the conversation has already begun.

questions.prompt: Why use straightforward language in a telephone message?
questions.answer: D — To ensure the message is understood.
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
Clarity allows the intended recipient to understand and act on it.

questions.prompt: Express Sangatiti’s gift-giving habit.
questions.answer: C — Sangatiti buys a present for his wife.
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
Present simple buys describes a habit; the other forms express completion or a current action.

questions.prompt: “Had Yusuph paid the dowry, he would have married Sikitu” implies what?
questions.answer: C is the intended choice: he did not pay the dowry and therefore did not marry her in that past situation.
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
Had Yusuph paid is an inverted third conditional, equivalent to if he had paid. It describes an unreal past condition.
questions.tip: The printed option says “cannot marry”, but the conditional concerns an unreal past event. It does not prove that a future marriage is impossible.

questions.prompt: Which technique helps you capture a lecture efficiently?
questions.answer: A — Use symbols, short forms and main ideas.
steps: Identify the tense, purpose or implication being tested.
Concise notes allow attention to meaning without trying to transcribe every sentence.

questions.prompt: Give a category name for Car, lorry, tractor, motorcycle.
steps: Find the class shared by the items, rather than a number of them.

questions.prompt: Give a category name for Pen, pencil, ruler, exercise book.

questions.prompt: Give a category name for Table, chair, cupboard, door.
questions.answer: Furniture is the intended category for table, chair and cupboard; a door is normally a building fixture.
steps: Find the class shared by the items, rather than a number of them.
The first three are furniture. The inclusion of door makes the set imprecise in ordinary classification.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
This is an objectively verifiable description of the disease’s cause.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: The disease affects people in different ways.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
Variation in symptoms and severity is observable.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: Some doctors believe the disease is man-made.
questions.answer: OPINION, for the expressed belief in this exercise.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
Believe identifies the claim as a belief rather than evidence establishing its content.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: Most infected people develop mild to moderate illness.
questions.answer: FACT, in the examination’s general description.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
This is a testable population-level statement, also reflected in WHO’s general overview.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: It seems that many recover without hospitalisation.
questions.answer: OPINION, under the exercise’s wording-based distinction.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
It seems frames the statement as the speaker’s impression, even though recovery without hospitalisation can also be measured.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: People should keep a safe distance, including from people without visible illness.
questions.answer: FACT is the likely intended classification as evidence-based preventive guidance; the word should also makes this a recommendation rather than a purely descriptive fact.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
Distinguish support for a preventive measure from the grammatical form of advice. A strict fact-versus-value classification could call the recommendation an opinion.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: Dar es Salaam might be the most affected region.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
Might expresses an unverified possibility; no regional data is supplied.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: There is a great possibility it is a respiratory disease.
questions.answer: OPINION, because of the speculative framing.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
Possibility marks uncertainty in the sentence; this classification concerns the wording, not whether COVID-19 actually causes respiratory illness.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: Symptoms include fever, tiredness, cough and loss of taste or smell.
questions.answer: FACT, as a description of recognised symptoms.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
These symptoms can be clinically observed. Their relative frequency varies, so the supplied wording should not be treated as a current ranking.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: Classify the supplied sentence: My view is that lockdown cannot help much.
steps: Look for a verifiable description or wording signalling belief, uncertainty or recommendation.
My view explicitly marks a personal judgement.
questions.tip: This question tests the language of fact and opinion. A factual-sounding sentence still needs evidence; a cautious phrase can describe a scientifically supported idea.

questions.prompt: My mother does not like ___ (lay) on a blanket.
questions.answer: lying is correct natural English. Laying is the mechanical -ing form of printed lay, but it needs an object and does not fit the intended resting meaning.
steps: Use an -ing activity after the preference verb to match the passage’s construction.
The correct base verb for resting on a blanket is lie, whose -ing form is lying. Lay means put something down: laying a blanket, for example.
questions.tip: Love, like and hate can also take to-infinitives in many of these sentences. The -ing forms give a consistent model; enjoy would require an -ing complement.

questions.prompt: Join the woman and her daughter’s examination success using whose.
questions.answer: That woman, whose daughter passed her final examination outstandingly, is our family friend.
steps: Preserve the original participants and meaning while applying the requested linker.
Whose links the daughter to the woman. Commas mark the added information.

questions.prompt: Join the cloudy weather and absence of rain using despite.

questions.prompt: As Kulwa, write to your sister Milembe about Masanja’s graduation in Language Teaching at the University of Dar es Salaam next month, which all the family plans to attend.
questions.answer:
P.O. Box 120,
Dar es Salaam.
10 October 2025

Dear Milembe,
How are you? I hope you are well. I am writing to share the good news that our brother, Masanja, will graduate in Language Teaching at the University of Dar es Salaam next month. We are very proud of his hard work.
All the members of our family are planning to attend the graduation ceremony. We would be happy if you could join us to celebrate his achievement. Please let us know your travel plans so that we can make arrangements together.
I will send you the exact date and time as soon as the university confirms the details. Give my greetings to everyone at home. I look forward to seeing you at the ceremony.

Your loving brother,
Kulwa
steps: Use a personal address and date, Dear Milembe, a friendly body and a suitable closing. The example address and writing date may be replaced.
Include the brother’s name, programme, university, next-month timing and the whole family’s intention to attend.
Sign Kulwa. Since the paper supplies no ceremony date or time, promise to share them when confirmed rather than present invented event details as facts.
questions.tip: The sender’s address and writing date are model details. The graduation information is retained exactly from the question.

summaries.Section A — Objective questions: Match question tags to tense. A third conditional describes an unreal past event; it does not determine every future possibility.
summaries.Section B — Language use: Fact and opinion depend on both wording and evidence. Check the meaning of lie and lay, and use noun phrases after despite.
summaries.Section C — Letter writing: An informal letter combines clear information with a personal greeting and closing. Preserve supplied event details and sign the requested name.

labelling_note: The key explains overlapping options in 1(iv), the past-time meaning of 1(ix), the calendar mismatch in 5, and the inaccurate printed verb lay in 8(viii). Fact/opinion answers distinguish the exercise’s intended classification from strict descriptive versus advisory wording.
